entries.title: Nigerian military plane crash kills all 25 on board
entries.summary: Rescue teams searched the crash site after the military aircraft went down in southern Nigeria, with everyone on board now confirmed to have died.
entries.content:
Nigeria

Nigerian military plane crash kills all 25 on board

Published October 5, 2026last updated October 6, 2026

Rescue teams searched the crash site after the military aircraft went down in southern Nigeria, with everyone on board now confirmed to have died.

Nigerian authorities on Tuesday revised the death toll from a military aircraft crash in southern Nigeria to 25, down from the 32 initially reported, and said there were no survivors.

"NAF 931 had 25 persons on board, comprising five ‌crew members and 20 passengers," Nigerian ​Air Force (NAF) said ‌in ​a statement.

Nigerian President Bola Tinubu extended his "deepest condolences" to the deceased's loved ones. 

The aircraft was on a routine mission to Lagos, Nigeria's economic hub, when it crashed in the Igbokoda area of Ondo state, Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo said in a statement.

Wreckage located

Keyamo said the aircraft disappeared from radar at around 9 a.m. local time (7:00 a.m. GMT) and was later found to have crashed about halfway through its journey from Edo state to Lagos.

He said the wreckage had been located near a naval base.

The Nigerian Air Force identified the aircraft as an ATR-42 and said an immediate search and rescue operation had been launched.

A video circulating on social media showed a small crowd gathered near a river as rescuers searched the area by boat.

Locals told AP news agency about what they had heard and seen.

"The plane cleared some trees. We found some body parts, some clothes and shoes," one of the locals said.

UPDATE: The initial version of this story on Monday, October 5 had the death toll at 32, as reported by Nigerian officials. This has been amended following the updates on Tuesday.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery, Rob Turner

entries.title: Kenya reports first-ever Ebola death
entries.summary: The patient arrived in Kenya over the weekend from the Democratic Republic of Congo before testing positive for the virus. Health authorities are on high alert and monitoring for more cases.
entries.content:
October 6, 2026

The patient arrived in Kenya over the weekend from the Democratic Republic of Congo before testing positive for the virus. Health authorities are on high alert and monitoring for more cases.

Kenyan health authorities announced the country's first death from Ebola on Tuesday.

Health Minister Aden Duale said a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo died after returning to Kenya via Uganda over the weekend.

It makes Kenya the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in the DRC in mid-May. Neighboring Uganda has reported 20 cases and France has lodged one.

What did the Health Ministry say about the case?

Duale told reporters the deceased patient fell ill about a month ago and had been receiving treatment in the DRC. He then traveled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before taking a flight to Nairobi on October 3.

The patient was suffering "fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites," Duale said.

The man subsequently tested positive for Ebola and died Monday night. He was expected to be buried later on Tuesday in line with public health recommendations.

The health minister said 28 people who came into contact with the patient — including relatives and health workers — had been identified and would be quarantined. Another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the flight from Uganda were also being traced, he added.

"I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease," he said.

What is the status of the outbreak?

Congolese authorities officially declared an Ebola outbreak on May 15, but experts believe the virus may have already been circulating for some time before that point.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has recorded more than 4,000 Ebola deaths out of 8,400 cases since then.

The current Ebola outbreak is the fastest-growing in history, and the WHO has warned it could also become the deadliest because poor health resources and ongoing violence in the DRC have hampered efforts to contain it.

The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare type of Ebola that has no approved vaccine or treatment.

Ebola is spread between people by direct contact with bodily fluids. It can cause fever, fatigue, and muscle pain, followed by vomiting and diarrhea. Some patients also develop internal or external bleeding.

The disease has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Fact check: Misleading claims spark plague fears in Russia
entries.summary: The death of a lab worker at a plague research institute in Russia has sparked claims about a lab accident, hundreds of infections and international spread. Some of these viral narratives are misleading.
entries.content:
October 6, 2026

The death of a lab worker at a plague research institute in Russia has sparked claims about a lab accident, hundreds of infections and international spread. Some of these viral narratives are misleading.

Dozens of people were reportedly placed under observation after a laboratory worker at a Russian institute dedicated to studying plague and other infectious diseases died of severe pneumonia.

The case quickly became the subject of intense speculation on social media. Posts have ranged from expressions of fear and comparisons with the COVID-19 pandemic to claims about the laboratory incident that have not been substantiated.

DW Fact Check has examined several of the claims circulating online.

Alleged plague lab accident in Irkutsk remains unproven

Claim: "For those who don't get it: in Irkutsk, a lab technician broke a flask containing the plague virus and became infected with the disease, dying a few days later," a user posted on X in Russian. "This happened on September 25, and by October 2, she was already dead. In the meantime, she had infected several hundred people." The post, which included a photo of the alleged laboratory worker, garnered over 320,000 views.

DW Fact check: Unproven

There is no independent evidence confirming that a leak of the plague pathogen occurred at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East.

On the contrary, Russia's public health authority, Rospotrebnadzor, said that two commissions investigating biosafety procedures at the institute found "no evidence of an accident involving pathogenic microorganisms." The Russian news agency TASS, citing Rospotrebnadzor, also reported that tests on the deceased employee detected no microorganisms linked to her professional activity.

Some social media users have tried to debunk the claim about a broken test tube, pointing to safety standards in high-containment laboratories, where the use of glassware may be restricted or completely banned to reduce the risk of accidents.

The Irkutsk institute does work with highly pathogenic microorganisms, including strains classified in Russia's highest pathogenicity groups, such as Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague.

However, DW could not independently verify the formally designated biosafety level of the institute's laboratories. Biosafety level, or BSL, is an international classification describing the containment measures required when handling dangerous pathogens, with BSL-4 reserved for the most hazardous agents.

DW asked the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute to comment on the alleged incident and its laboratory safety procedures but had received no response by the time of publication.

WHO website update unrelated to the Russian case

Claim: "The WHO appears to have updated its fact sheet on plague the same day the Irkutsk lab worker presented at hospital, with (probably) the plague." This claim appeared in a number of posts on X, each reaching thousands of users.

DW Fact check: Misleading

The World Health Organization (WHO) updated its plague fact sheet on the same day the Russian laboratory worker was hospitalized, but no evidence links the two events.

According to media reports, the laboratory worker may have been exposed to Yersinia pestis around September 25. Four days later, on September 29, she was hospitalized in Shelekhov with severe respiratory symptoms.

The WHO updated its plague fact sheet on September 29, the same day it published a news release on global trends in cholera, meningitis and plague. The update was part of a broader WHO publication cycle on infectious disease.

The release reported global surveillance data covering 2019 to 2025 and said the findings were published in the latest edition of the Weekly Epidemiological Record, which was released on September 25.

The timing therefore appears coincidental. The previous version of the WHO's plague fact sheet, accessible as an archived page, was dated July 7, 2022.

The social media account sharing the claim also changed its name in October to one that suggests it is reporting live from Irkutsk. Its profile describes itself as providing "sourced updates on the Irkutsk lab leak" and "latest news as it breaks live." However, the account's profile indicates that it was created in May and is based in Australia.

Such accounts can emerge quickly during breaking news events, presenting themselves as local or specialist sources while sharing unverified information.

Old video falsely linked to current plague claims in Russia

Claim: As news of the plague spreads, some old videos are being repurposed, adding to the disinformation. In one such video posted on X, a user claimed that the plague has also spread to other parts of Russia. The caption in Russian reads, "The plague marches across Russia. God has heard our prayers!"

DW Fact check: Misleading

The video is old and unrelated to the current developments in Irkutsk. A reverse image search reveals that the video was initially posted on August 31 this year, claiming that it showed the Russian republic of Kabardino-Balkaria, a tourist destination around 6,000 kilometers (3,700 miiles)from Irkutsk.

The old video has been viewed more than 1.7 million times on Instagram. The same video was also posted on Telegram. The Russian news agency TASS reported on August 31 that the plague pathogen had been detected in local squirrels and that the area had been closed to tourists.

In the video, a person can be heard saying, "It's at the turnoff from the paved road toward Serebryany Istochnik" in Russian. Serebryany Istochnik, or Silver Spring, is a spring located in the Dzhily-Su area in Kabardino-Balkaria.

The situation in the Irkutsk region is still being investigated, but there are no confirmed reports of a plague outbreak in Russia. Health authorities have introduced precautionary measures following the death of the laboratory worker, while tests are reportedly being carried out.

Edited by: Joscha Weber

entries.title: AI models keep hacking real systems during tests. What does this mean?
entries.summary: AI models have repeatedly broken into real commercial and government systems during safety tests during 2026. Cybersecurity researcher Thorsten Holz explains what that means, and why he isn't expecting a robot uprising.
entries.content:
October 6, 2026

AI models have repeatedly broken into real commercial and government systems during safety tests during 2026. Cybersecurity researcher Thorsten Holz explains what that means, and why he isn't expecting a robot uprising.

Let's start with people's real world fears about AI. Here's a sample of people we asked:

Sebastian, 22, says it'll be an AI-powered robot uprising that finally wipes out humanity: "I think that'll take some time," he says, admitting his dystopia owes a lot to the 2004 film "I, Robot."

Luisa, 19, has heard the rumors too. Her fear is what happens when these tools get into the wrong hands. "I'm more afraid of people," she says. "Powerful people."

Pilar, 25, is pessimistic about humanity's prospects. "The world is going down," she says. "Hopefully after my lifetime."

In 2026, AI systems have repeatedly slipped out of human control — and at some of the world's largest AI companies. 

What happens when AI agents go rogue?

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta have all disclosed in 2026 that their AI agents escaped the controlled test environments.

Agents are AI systems that don't just answer questions but act — running code, browsing the web, clicking through systems — on their own.

Thorsten Holz, scientific director at the Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy in Germany, is among the researchers who test AI systems.

"It feels a bit crazy how powerful these models have become." Holz told DW. "I didn't anticipate they'd be so obsessed with solving tasks and that they'd start to do things we never [foresaw]."

Holz is one of 16 authors of ExploitGym. ExploitGym is an AI benchmark published in May 2026 by a team led by the University of California, Berkeley, with researchers from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. It is a standardized test of cybersecurity capabilities and vulnerabilities.

Its 898 challenges test whether AI agents can turn known software bugs into working attacks. Each one runs inside a sandbox — a sealed-off digital space, cut off from the internet, so nothing the agent does can reach anything real. That's the theory, anyway.

In July, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI models had escaped from their sandbox.

They were running an internal ExploitGym test with the models' safety refusals switched off, a setting that lets evaluators measure what a model is capable of rather than what it will decline to do.

Failing the task, the models went looking for a shortcut instead, and found a flaw in the software meant to keep them sealed in. It let them onto the open internet.

From there they worked out that Hugging Face, a site where AI developers store and share models and data, probably held the answer to the test.

So, they broke in and went looking for it, organizing the effort on message boards they set up themselves. The behavior was not instructed, according to OpenAI's account of the incident.

Hugging Face detected the intrusion and shut it down before OpenAI connected it to its own test. No customer data was reportedly taken.

"What happened is really a bit of science fiction," Holz said.

Then, Google confirmed that its Gemini model had guessed or found login credentials and accessed three real companies' websites during a May test run by the independent evaluator Irregular — an intrusion Google learned of in July 2026 and disclosed weeks later.

Anthropic's and Meta's escapes happened in sandboxes run by the same firm, which has said it notified the labs in late July 2026 and that it has since fixed the flaws.

In late September 2026, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent had broken into a statistics portal belonging to Medicare, Australia's public health system, reaching non-public files and writing data into a government server. No patient records were reportedly touched. 

Could AI decide to wipe out humanity?

The incidents have revived older fears. If agents can program each other, where does that end? Could it lead to what philosopher Nick Bostrom has called a "paperclip maximizer"?

Bostrom's thought experiment imagines a machine given one simple goal: Make as many paperclips as possible.

The machine pursues the task so single-mindedly that it eventually treats humans as raw material standing in the way.

"For the intermediate future, I do not see any kind of scientific evidence that there could be this super intelligence that autonomously decides, 'Okay, let's kill,'" said Holz.

Rogue software needs vast datacenters to run, he said, which makes it visible. And the internet is built from parts that can keep working independently of one another.

But the AI escapes and hacks in 2026 were noticed late. Google learned of Gemini's intrusions two months after they happened, and OpenAI told Australia about the Medicare breach nearly three months after the event.

Holz said he expects a different kind of threat: Bad actors turning capable AI on critical infrastructure, mass compromise of ordinary machines, or chatbots used to manipulate information at scale and destabilize politics.

Can Europe compete with US and Chinese AI?

No, Europe cannot easily compete with China, according to experts.

France's Mistral and Germany's open-source Soofi project lag behind the frontier labs — a handful of US and Chinese firms building the most advanced models. Europe lacks the datacenter capacity to train systems at that scale, which leaves it dependent on non-European models, and largely subject to US or Chinese export controls. 

For Holz, the more pressing gap is expertise. "What we definitely need to see is how we can build up more competence in the area of security, AI, and especially the intersection of both," he said.

How worried should you be about AI?

Be skeptical of what the companies themselves claim, Holz said. They have a financial interest in the conversation, he said, particularly ahead of a stock market listing. "There's also fear mongering, or a bit of hype, about how advanced these models get."

Holz uses AI daily, as do his children. His nine-year-old generates coloring book pages. His 12-year-old uses it for homework, but has already learned the hard way that it lies and that "it's sometimes wrong."

This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted. You can subscribe to the podcast here.

entries.title: Nobel Physics Prize goes to Francis Halzen for neutrino work
entries.summary: Halzen got the Nobel for his contributions to the IceCube neutrino Observatory and discovery of high-energy neutrinos, described as "ghostly messengers from space."
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

Nobel Physics Prize goes to Francis Halzen for neutrino work

October 6, 2026

Halzen got the Nobel for his contributions to the IceCube neutrino Observatory and discovery of high-energy neutrinos, described as "ghostly messengers from space."

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences on Tuesday awarded the Nobel Prize in physics to Francis Halzen.

He received the award for this "decisive contributions to the IceCube neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin," the academy said.

The committee described the neutrinos as "ghostly messengers from space."

What Francis Halzen said about his Nobel prize

Born in Belgium, the 82-year-old is a physics professor University of Wisconsin–Madison in the United States. Halzen acknowleged the prize as he was called on the phone by the panelists who presented the award.

He told the Nobel academy that he was "surprised" to get the prize and thanked the many contributors to the project, adding that the discoveries required a lot of "luck."

"This was kind of an adventure, where success was not guaranteed. It was a long journey, but it finally worked," Halzen said.

The Belgian scientist said that he hoped his Nobel Prize reflects on the "really courageous people" who believed in the project. "No really respectable conservative physicists would have joined me, but many talented people did, and that's why I'm here," Halzen added.

Belgium's Prime Minister Bart De Wever extended his "heartfelt congratulations" to Halzen. He noted that Halzen is the 11th Belgian to win a Nobel, and the second in physics.

What is the IceCube neutrino Observatory?

Neutrinos are tiny cosmic particles of ultra small mass that are present everywhere. They come from stars like the sun and trillions of them pass through our bodies every second.

Scientists are not able to observe the so-called ghost particles zooming around on their own, so they measure what happens when they collide with other bits of matter.

Halzen's idea of capturing neutrinos at the Earth's South Pole dates back to the 1980s. The IceCube Neutrino Observatory was subsequently built at the South Pole in Antarctica as a dedicated facility to capture and study the neutrinos.

"The neutrinos we detect are like fingerprints that help us understand the objects and phenomena where the neutrinos are produced," the group said.

"IceCube collaborators address several big questions in physics, like the nature of dark matter and the properties of the neutrino itself," the organization says.

Some 450 physicists from 58 institutions in 14 countries make up the IceCube collaboration.

The Nobel prizes awarded this week

The physics prize has been awarded 119 times to 230 laureates between 1901 and 2025.

Last year, it went to three scientists for their research on the strange behavior of subatomic particles called quantum tunneling that enabled the ultra-sensitive measurements achieved by MRI machines and laid the groundwork for better cellphones and faster computers.

It is the second Nobel announced this week, after the medicine prize was awarded to three scientists whose work on optogenetics has helped unravel how the brain works.

Further laureates are set to be named in chemistry, literature and peace in the days up to Friday.

The prizes will be presented at ceremonies on 10 December.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million; €1 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Germany faces a triple threat from Russia, China and domestic far-right extremists
entries.summary: At a rare public hearing Germany's intelligence agencies identified Russia as the country's most dangerous adversary. The threat from China is also coming into focus. And the homegrown far right also poses a challenge.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany's triple threat: Russia, China, far-right extremists

October 6, 2026

At a rare public hearing Germany's intelligence agencies identified Russia as the country's most dangerous adversary. The threat from China is also coming into focus. And the homegrown far right also poses a challenge.

The heads of Germany's intelligence agencies rarely provide information openly. What members of the Bundestag's Parliamentary Control Committee discuss in their bug-proof meeting room with the presidents of the Federal Intelligence Service, or Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), and the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), as well as the president of the Military Counterintelligence Service, is strictly confidential.

Since 2016, however, a public meeting has been held once a year, open to journalists, as well as citizens who register in advance. At this year's meeting, held Monday, intelligence officials seemed extremely alarmed. They painted a picture of a country in the midst of a confrontation with Russia.

"The military scenarios envisioned for the year 2029 have already become a reality today in the shadowy world of intelligence," BfV President Sinan Selen said, referring to a recent assessment by NATO experts that, under certain conditions, Russia could be capable of launching an attack on the alliance in a few years.

BND President Martin Jäger said there were no indications of an imminent military attack. Instead, Moscow is waging a "shadow war" through sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation, and espionage. "No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany," Jäger explained, adding: "Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia."

In Russia's crosshairs

Germany plays an essential role in supporting Ukrainethrough military, financial and humanitarian efforts. Jäger said that this makes Russia see Germany as a "major obstacle to Russia's hegemonic power projection in Europe." "If Germany were to falter, all of Europe — and Europe's support for Ukraine — would begin to unravel," Jäger concluded.

The intelligence agency heads expressed concern over the course of the war in Ukraine. Russia is expected to step up the pressure on the country this coming winter. At the same time, Moscow is attempting to hinder Western arms deliveries.

The intelligence services find that Russia is deliberately attempting to create uncertainty and weaken societal resilience in the European Union and elsewhere. Selen spoke of "coldly calculated destabilization operations."

When asked whether Germany would be safer if it did less to support Ukraine, Jäger said unequivocally that aid to Kyiv is in the national interest.

In addition to espionage, there are an increasing number of acts of sabotage and even assassination operations. Transportation routes, military infrastructure, and the defense industry are particularly at risk.

As an example, authorities cited this summer's attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, in which Russia is the prime suspect. In August, a drone rigged with explosives was discovered there near a Ukrainian cargo plane. Selen, head of the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany's domestic intelligence agency, again pointed to clear evidence of Russian involvement.

'Disposable agents' and organized crime

Germany's domestic intelligence agency is particularly concerned about the increasing use of so-called low-level agents, or people who are recruited locally via digital channels, for example, for espionage, transport services or acts of sabotage. "Social media plays a central role here," Selen stressed.

The intelligence chiefs also said Russian services were collaborating with organized crime groups. An increase in this area is a development that security agency heads say they will need to prepare for more thoroughly in the future.

According to the BND, Russia is gradually pushing boundaries through targeted actions. Examples cited included drone overflights of NATO territory and airspace violations in Moldova. "Russia is very deliberately shifting the bar here toward a kind of new normal," said Jäger.

Jäger said covert operations against individual NATO countries, particularly in the Baltic states, were conceivable, recalling events in Crimea in 2014, when Russian troops appeared as covert units without any insignia. Now the agency heads suggest similar operations could be conducted to test the alliance's ability to respond.

China's long-term challenge

In addition to Russia, China continues to be a concern for security agencies. The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution once again warned against attempts to gain access to German know-how through research collaborations and universities. Particular focus is on artificial intelligence, quantum technology, hypersonic technology and biotechnology.

The authorities are also watching the spread of Chinese technology products with concern. Data leaks from connected vehicles or household appliances could be misused. In extreme cases, it is even conceivable that systems could be shut down remotely.

Right-wing extremism on the rise

The topic of extremism also took up a significant portion of the discussion with the parliamentary committee. Regarding right-wing extremism, Selen spoke of an "extremely alarming trend" toward groups of young actors who are prone to violence and are increasingly forming international networks.

MAD President Martina Rosenberg reported an increase in suspected cases of extremism within the Bundeswehr. The increasing radicalization of society is not sparing the armed forces either.

Against the backdrop of growing threats, the heads of the BND and BfV defended a planned expansion of intelligence powers. The plan is to significantly expand agencies' powers regarding the collection, storage, and automated analysis of data. In addition, the agencies are to be given the ability for the first time, to actively combat threats such as acts of sabotage or hacker attacks through counterattacks.

"Amid geopolitical instability, conflict-prone systemic rivalry and hybrid aggression, there is a greater need than ever for tailored capabilities and robust security systems," Selen said.

Jäger said: "If we have these powers, then we will use them. And our adversaries will feel the consequences."

Critics in Germany, however, warn against blurring the line between intelligence gathering and police intervention. In light of these expanding powers, Konstantin von Notz, a member of the Parliamentary Control Panel with the opposition environmentalist Greens, is also calling for greater oversight of the intelligence services. He expects the Federal Constitutional Court to address the plan to expand the powers of the intelligence services.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: France: Trade unions join students in major demonstration
entries.summary: Tens of thousands are expected at nationwide protests against poor learning conditions for students in France.
entries.content:
France

France: Trade unions join students in major demonstration

October 6, 2026

Tens of thousands are expected at nationwide protests against poor learning conditions for students in France.

A day of nationwide blockades and street protests are planned on Tuesday in France, led by high-school and trade union groups. Tens of thousands are expected to take to the streets.

The demonstrations are part of a movement that sprung in recent weeks demanding that French President Emmanuel Macron's government tackle understaffed and underfunded schools.

Protests that began in Paris's deprived suburbs have now spread across the country, including pupils from affluent areas who have joined in solidarity.

Hundreds of high school entrances have been blocked by student protesters since late September. The students have decried poor learning conditions, such as missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that are not suitable for high temperatures.

While many of the demonstrations have been peaceful, some protesters have lit trash can fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police, who have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds, with authorities accusing the movement of having devolved into urban violence.

Police accused of brutality towards children

The country's Justice Ministry said that 5,060 people have been arrested since the protests began. Some 87% of those taken into custody were minors.

Over 1,800 people face charges, including 1,483 minors, the ministry said, without ​providing details of what they had been accused of, although some 790 cases have alaready been dismissed.

Trade unions and human rights groups have accused the police of using disproportionate force on children. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Monday that police have launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started.

Among the reports, a 15-year-old lost his hand at a protest in the northern town of Lens, a 16-year-old lost the use of his right eye after being seriously injured in the head in the central town of Tours, while in Saint-Ouen-L'Aumone, northwest of Paris, a 14-year-old lost most of his teeth when a police officer appeared to fire a projectile at him at very close range.

Government promises response

French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said he had ‌ordered government ministers to study the students' leading demands.

Among the demands the government will be tackling are ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the ‌length ​of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day and the need for longer lunch breaks.

The government has promised to also look at repairs needed to ageing school buildings.

Lecornu said ministers are expected to submit their first proposals by the end of October. The ​protests have put pressure on a government that has sought to narrow a ballooning budget deficit.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Germany's ex-spy chief arrested for espionage
entries.summary: August Hanning, the man who once led Germany's spy service, is now under investigation for passing on state secrets.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany's ex-spy chief arrested for espionage

October 6, 2026

August Hanning, the man who once led Germany's spy service, is now under investigation for passing on state secrets.

Police have arrested the former head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence agency, August Hanning, on suspicion of espionage, the federal prosecutor's office announced Tuesday.

Hanning served as the agency's chief from December 1998 to November 2005 before moving to the Federal Interior Ministry, where he worked as state secretary until November 2009.

According to a statement from the prosecutor's office, the 80-year-old faces charges including espionage, disclosure of state secrets, attempted treason and working as a secret service agent.

It did not say which foreign intelligence service he is suspected of working for.

The statement added that another former high-ranking BND employee was also arrested on suspicion of providing hundreds of classified documents to Hanning after his tenure as spy chief ended in exchange for payment.

DW's chief political editor Michaela Küfner, reporting from a government press briefing on the arrest, described the case as Germany's "biggest espionage scandal of the century."

What else do we know about the investigation?

Police arrested Hanning early Tuesday at his home in Nordwalde near the western German city of Münster, according to information from WDR, NDR and the daily Süddeutsche Zeitung.

Hanning's alleged accomplice, who was identified only as Manfred D. in line with Germany's privacy laws, was taken into custody in Bavaria.

Authorities were conducting searches at both suspects' properties, as well as in Berlin, the prosecutor said.

During Hanning's tenure as spy head, D. served as his chief of staff. He also subsequently worked under Hanning at the Interior Ministry until 2009.

He is facing charges of "aiding and abetting attempted treason and espionage against the state."

Marc Henrichmann, who chairs the German parliament's intelligence oversight committee, said following the arrests that Germany "will not tolerate the betrayal of secrets."

"Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out," he said in comments to the AFP news agency.

German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz, also a member of the oversight committee, said the allegations were "deeply troubling" and called for a "swift and thorough investigation."

The investigation into Hanning reportedly began due to his connection to a high-profile trial involving businesswoman Christine Block.

2,000 documents allegedly handed over to Hanning

The prosecutor's office said Hanning and Manfred D. are believed to have come up with their arrangement in 2010.

From 2012 to March 2026, D. served as chief of staff to Hanning's successors at the BND spy agency, where he had access to a wealth of classified documents, according to the prosecutor's statement.

"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement said.

It added that D. is alleged to have provided Hanning with information until at least mid-2022, and that Hanning used that information in his private consulting work.

Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D., for several years," the statement said.

The two suspects are expected to appear before an investigating judge on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Canada: Quebec separatists return to power, promise new independence referendum
entries.summary: Parti Quebecois has won the provincial election, but fallen short of a majority. Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he will seek another referendum on independence, but not while US President Donald Trump is in office.
entries.content:
Canada

Canada: Quebec separatists win vote, promise referendum

October 6, 2026

Parti Quebecois has won the provincial election, but fallen short of a majority. Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he will seek another referendum on independence, but not while US President Donald Trump is in office.

In Quebec's provincial election on Monday, the separatist Parti Quebecois (PQ) came in the lead after promising another referendum on independence from Canada but fell short of a outright majority.

The PQ, led by 49-year-old Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, was on track to win nearly 60 of the 127 seats in the National Assembly, just short of the 64 needed for a majority.

However, their return to power after more than a decade comes with a caveat as the minority government will need support from opposition parties to pass legislation and survive confidence votes.

"Quebecers elected the Parti Quebecois asking it to work with the other parties, and I heard that message," the PQ leader said.

St-Pierre Plamondon says dreams of independent Quebec

The PQ's return to power also brings to forefront the issue of identity of Quebec's French-speakers, who make up 80% of the population, and comes with a promise of an independence referendum.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he envisioned Quebec as a country on its own and that a referendum would allow Quebecers to decide their own future.

"I continue to dream and visualize that country," St-Pierre Plamondon said in his victory speech. "That dream will be realized one day."

The jubilant leader, however, made it clear that the referendum would not take place while US President Donald Trump remains in office. He said the decision would need "an informed and calm debate" and could not be allowed to be "hijacked by the theatrics of an unpredictable president."

Severing ties with British monarchy?

The PQ's victory does not necessarily signal majority support for independence.

While in the last referendum for independence in 1995, just 50.58% voted to stay in Canada, recent polls show support for sovereignty at around 30%.

"If Quebec becomes independent it would make us politically, economically and militarily vulnerable," 19-year-old Alexia Gomez, told news agency AFP.

The Liberals and Conservatives have also voiced their opposition to an independence referendum, further complicating the PQ's path.

On the other hand, in a move more likely to find resonance among Quebecers, St-Pierre Plamondon's party has also pledged to reduce Quebec's ties to the British monarchy.

Monday's result comes just two weeks before Alberta voters decide whether to support beginning the process toward a referendum on separating from Canada.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Germany news: Far-right AfD gets first house speaker in a German state parliament
entries.summary: For the first time since World War II, a far-right party has a house speaker in a German state parliament. And Germany's foreign minister has warned that the climate crisis could fuel extremism. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Saxony-Anhalt elects AfD parliamentary speaker

Published October 6, 2026last updated October 6, 2026

For the first time since World War II, a far-right party has a house speaker in a German state parliament. And Germany's foreign minister has warned that the climate crisis could fuel extremism. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Tobias Rausch from the Alternative for Germany (AfD) has been elected as the far-right party's first speaker in a state parliament
  • Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has warned of the consequences of climate change in fragile states
  • A German-Russian man has been sent to prison in Latvia after being found guilty of aiding Russian military personnel
  • A former German spy chief has been arrested on charges of espionage and treason

Here is a look round at the latest news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, October 6, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Pope receives German Christmas cake gift by car from Saxony

Pope receives German Christmas cake gift by car from Saxony

A typical German Christmas speciality intended as a gift for Pope Leo XIV was driven to Rome in an official vehicle from the state of Saxony after it was deemed unsuitable for air transport, officials revealed on Tuesday.

The 4-kilogram (8.8-pound) cake, a so-called stollen, which was made in the Ore Mountains in eastern Germany, was taken by Saxon Premier Michael Kretschmer to the Vatican for a private audience at the end of September.

The cake was reportedly too large to be taken into the cabin and too fragile to be placed in the aircraft hold, the officials said.

No information was provided on the cost by the officials at the Saxon State Chancellery.

The vehicle also transported other presents and documents.

Skip next section Greens leader in Saxony-Anhalt says border has been crossed

Greens leader in Saxony-Anhalt says border has been crossed

The leader of the Green parliamentary party in Saxony-Anhalt, Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz, has vowed to defend democracy following the election of a member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), Tobias Rausch, as parliamentary speaker.

The election of the member of a confirmed right-wing extremist, anti-constitutional party as house speaker meant that a "border" had been crossed, she said.

"We will not allow ourselves to be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights here or those of the people in this state are to be curtailed," she added.

Earlier in her address, she said that if the AfD were to take power in the state, her party would "speak out if people were denigrated because of their origins, beliefs or lifestyle."

Sziborra-Seidlitz said Saxony-Anhalt could not afford for "exclusion to become the political brand of this parliament and our state."

The AfD emerged from September elections as the strongest single force in parliament but has so far failed to find parties willing to enter into a coalition with it.

The Saxony-Anhalt chapter of the party has been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the domestic intelligence agency in the state.

Among other things, the party advocates a hard-line anti-immigration agenda and an intolerant stance toward LGBTQ+ rights.

Skip next section Far-right AfD candidate elected state parliamentary speaker

Far-right AfD candidate elected state parliamentary speaker

Tobias Rausch, the far-right Alternative for Germany's (AFD's) nomination for speaker in Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament, has been elected with the help of the populist BSW party.

Rausch gained 48 votes in favor to 29 against from 82 eligible votes. There were five abstentions.

The AfD holds 39 seats in the parliament and the BSW five, giving Rausch the majority he needed to win the post, as the other parties combined — all of which reject working with the AfD — also hold 39 seats.

The result, however, means that members of parties besides the AfD and BSW voted for him.

Rausch, 35, thus becomes the first member of the AfD — a party classified by domestic intelligence in Saxony-Anhalt as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization — to become speaker in a state parliament in Germany.

The new speaker is a real-estate entrepreneur by profession and has been a member of parliament for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt since 2016.

The parliamentary session was accompanied by several anti-AfD protests in front of the parliament building.

The vote for speaker is separate from that for state premier.

The AfD's lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, who won the September election with 44% of the vote — thus falling short of an absolute majority — intends to stand for the position in December.

As no other party so far wants to form a coalition with his party, it is still in question whether he can win a vote or form a government.

The AfD says it is in dialogue with the BSW and individual parliamentarians to seek the necessary support.



Skip next section EU chief warns against German-led push to cut budget

EU chief warns against German-led push to cut budget

Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, warned on Tuesday against major cuts to the European Union's next long-term budget. 

"I am aware that balancing all of these constraints is not easy. I am also aware of the difficult budgetary situation in the member states," von der Leyen told the European Parliament in the French city of Strasbourg.

"But I would like to caution against large cuts. They would risk undermining critical priorities that we have all agreed upon," she added.

Negotiations on the long-term budget for the 2028-2034 period are currently underway. The EU's long-term budget, also known as the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), is the European Union's seven-year spending plan that sets how much the bloc can spend and on which priorities, such as agriculture, regional development, research, defense, migration, and climate policy. 

The European Commission has proposed a budget of around €1.76 trillion (about $1.98 trillion). The budget is financed mainly through contributions based on the size of member states' economies. 

The current MFF for 2021-2027 amounts to around €1.2 trillion.

Traditionally, Germany has opposed increases to the proposed budget, while other countries favor maintaining subsidies for economically disadvantaged regions. This time has been no different, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz calling for major cuts.

Ireland, which currently holds the rotating EU presidency, is expected to present a new compromise proposal in the coming days. 

European Council President Antonio Costa aims to secure an agreement on the new budget by the end of the year.

Skip next section Applications to refuse military service on the rise

Applications to refuse military service on the rise

The number of applications from people wishing to refuse military service on grounds of conscience has risen sharply.

Altogether 12,102 such applications were made in the first eighth months of the year, according to figures from the Federal Office for Family Affairs and Civil Society Functions (BAFzA) — more than triple the number in the whole of 2025 (3,879).

The sharp increase comes after Germany's new military service law came into effect on January 1.

That law foresees mandatory medical screening for young men born in 2008 or later, with an eye to recruiting volunteers to expand the armed forces.

Although compulsory military service has been suspended in Germany since 2011, it remains enshrined in Germany's Basic Law.

The right to refuse armed military service as a conscientious objector also remains in place.

Parliament can decide to introduce needs-based conscription if recruitment targets are not reached under the current voluntary system.

Skip next section German Economy: Recovery faces setback as factory orders plunge

German Economy: Recovery faces setback as factory orders plunge

In August, orders from German factories fell faster than expected, marking the first decline in four months. Orders were down 10.6% compared to July. 

According to the statistics agency Destatis, the decline in orders from large German manufacturers highlights the fragility of the recovery in Europe's largest economy. 

Germany's economy has been stagnant for an extended period and has only been recovering slowly, supported by massive public spending. However, recent data have shown signs of strengthening. 

The German Economy Ministry said that August's orders data represented a "significant setback." It also noted that, excluding the drop in large orders, the overall situation was virtually unchanged from July.

The August decline was driven by weaker domestic demand. Orders fell by more than 60% in the category that includes military vehicles, aircraft, ships, and trains.

Germany raises military spending

Orders in this sector have increased as Germany spends vast sums on its military to confront an increasingly hostile Russia and amid concerns about US security guarantees for Europe. 

The ministry stressed that the growing importance of public procurement has made orders "highly volatile."

By comparison, new orders from June to August were 1.3% higher than in the previous three-month period.

The energy crisis stemming from the conflict in the Middle East has created additional challenges for Germany's economic recovery, but the economy has weathered the impact better than initially feared. 

Experts recently doubled their growth forecast for this year to 1.3%.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Ex-spy chief August Hanning arrested for espionage — reports

IN DEPTH: Ex-spy chief August Hanning arrested for espionage — reports

August Hanning, who served as the head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence agency from 1998 to 2005, has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, according to various media sources.

DW will keep you up to date with the latest developments in the case in this article: Germany: Ex-spy chief arrested for espionage — reports

Skip next section Police rush to Lower Saxony school after rampage alarm sounded

Police rush to Lower Saxony school after rampage alarm sounded

Police in Lower Saxony have been deployed to a high school in the town of Langwedel after being alerted to a possible rampage attack by an alarm, according various German media.

Later, officers confirmed that the situation was resolved. It remained unclear if a false alarm was triggered or if a serious security threat had been brought under control.

Skip next section German-Russian man jailed over helping Russian military

German-Russian man jailed over helping Russian military

A German-Russian man has been sentenced in Latvia to seven years in prison and one year on probation after being found guilty of collecting and supplying money and goods to Russian military personnel.

The man was detained by Latvian authorities while on one of his car trips allegedly transporting the goods across the Latvian-Russian border.

The man denied supplying sanctioned goods, saying he was transporting humanitarian aid such as wheelchairs, crutches and nappies.

The Latvian news agency LETA cited the responsible court in Riga as having said he was in fact carrying goods including night-vision devices and telescopes.

Prosecutors used correspondence, photographs and videos found on the man's mobile phone to back their case against him.

The verdict against the man, who holds both German and Russian citizenship, is not yet final and can be appealed.

Skip next section Wadephul warns of climate change as security risk

Wadephul warns of climate change as security risk

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has highlighted the consequences of climate change for global security as the Berlin Climate and Security Conference kicks off in the capital.

"Particularly in fragile states, climate change exacerbates poverty and hunger — and can thus also become a fertile ground for extremism and terrorism or lead to waves of migration," he said.

Wadephul also emphasized the importance of climate protection in enhancing national security.

"When Russia once more deliberately attacks the energy infrastructure in Ukraine, decentralized, renewable energy sources could become a form of life insurance," he said.

"Investment in climate protection is also investment in our security," he added.

The Berlin Climate and Security Conference, which has been held annually since 2019, brings together some 250 international actors in the fields of climate, peace and security.

Participants include representatives from countries particularly affected by climate change and from the UN, EU and scientific and civil society organizations.

Skip next section New Saxony-Anhalt parliament sits to choose speaker

New Saxony-Anhalt parliament sits to choose speaker

The newly elected state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt is poised to hold its first session on Tuesday, over four weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won elections there with almost 44% of the vote.

The AfD holds 39 seats in the legislature, the same number of seats as the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the Left Party, Greens and Social Democrats (SPD) together.

During the session, parliamentarians are to vote for a speaker, with the AfD, as the strongest force, empowered to nominate the first candidate.

The AfD has put forward long-serving parliamentarian Tobias Rausch, 35, for the post, a choice that the populist BSW, which holds 5 seats, has pledged to back.

All the other parties refuse to work with the AfD under a policy known as the "firewall," and the CDU chairman in the state has advised members of his party to abstain from the vote.

If Rausch is elected, he will become the first AfD speaker of a state parliament in Germany.

However, if he fails to be elected in a first round of voting, all the other parties can put forward their own candidates.

There will be no vote on who will lead the state.

The session will be accompanied by protests by civil society groups who see the AfD, which has been classified as a "confirmed extremist" organization by domestic intelligence in the state, as a danger to Germany's democracy.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

DW's newsroom in Bonn wishes all its readers guten Tag as much of Germany continues to experience what is here called a "golden October" of mild, sunny weather.

The new parliament in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt is poised to sit for the first time after elections in September handed a landslide victory to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

The session is being watched closely to see whether the AfD succeeds in installing its first speaker in a state parliament in Germany, with the populist BSW party pledging to back the AfD's nomination for the post.

One of Germany's top cultural events, the Frankfurt Book Fair, is also getting underway with preliminary events, including a press conference, before its doors open on Wednesday for specialist visitors.

And Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has warned that the climate crisis could undermine security and fuel new waves of migration as the Berlin Climate and Security Conference kicks off in the capital.
